## The Source Base

**This article's primary sources are the seventy articles that precede it.** Each was read by an extractor for a fixed set of facts, and each fact was tied to a quotation that a script then found verbatim in the article, 763 quotations in all with none failing. The coding decisions made on top of the ledger, 21 of them, carry quotations checked the same way. **The register of allocations was read from a saved copy and parsed into 532 rows**, with its officiality markup read at all three levels and its notes read for the sources of out-of-sequence numbers \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The register lists designators allocated after 19 August 1998, the date of the official list of that year \[[DOD 4120.15-L, 1998][ref_dod_412015l_1998]\], and the 2004 edition of the official list was read for whether it dates its research rows, which it does not \[[DOD 4120.15-L, 2004][ref_dod_412015l_2004]\]. The compiler's appendix of unmanned military X vehicles was read as a second source on crew \[[Parsch, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles, Appendix 4][ref_dusrm_app4]\], and his page of missing designations and his account of the allocation process as primaries on the anomalies and the procedure \[[Missing USAF and DOD Aircraft Designations][ref_missing_mds]\] \[[Allocation of Official Aerospace Vehicle MDS Designations][ref_mds_allocation]\]. **Eleven original papers of the statistical methods the article uses were read for their definitions**, Kendall, Wilson, Fisher on the exact test, on contingency tables and on the Poisson dispersion test, Cochran, Woolf, Shannon, Pielou, Dunn and Fleiss with his colleagues. The four editions of the numbering rule, of 1962, 1994, 2005 and 2020, were read by earlier articles and are cited here through them and directly \[[Air Force Regulation 66-11, 1962][ref_afr_66_11_1962]\] \[[Air Force Joint Instruction 16-401, 1994][ref_afji_16_401_1994]\] \[[Air Force Instruction 16-401, 2005][ref_afi_16_401_2005]\] \[[Department of the Air Force Instruction 16-401, 2020][ref_dafi_16_401_2020]\].

**The survey was harvested by 86 queries to the bibliographic index and 30 to the reports server**, giving a pool of 17,869 records of which 5,657 passed the gate into 12 clusters. The gate carries 23 keep cases and 39 refusal cases, each rerun with its spaces replaced by hyphens, and **the refusal cases were taken from what the queries returned**, alloy and refrigerant designation systems, zoological and chemical nomenclature, rapid prototyping of medical implants, a submarine research model that shares an agency's name, gene names that share an acronym, and geological maps of a flight test base. **Reading admitted samples found a defect in the gate itself**, a pattern meant to make a separator optional that instead made it lazy, so that unhyphenated words such as spaceplane and reentry were missed by the patterns written to catch them. It was found because a keep case was written unhyphenated, and it was fixed before the counts above were taken.

**One measurement was attempted and abandoned.** A count of report-server records naming each design number in their titles was meant to test the first article's claim that the record thins after 2000. The section headed What the Record Measures gives the three reasons it failed, and **no number from it appears in this article.**

## Epistemic State

### The Article's Own Vantage Point

**The article is dated 16 December 2025 and written on 3 October 2026.** Several of the facts it uses postdate its date. The X-68A and X-76A rows first appeared in the public register in January 2026, DARPA announced the X-76 on 9 March 2026, and the reason for the number 76 is known only from that announcement. **Every statement about the X-76's number, and the founding-year class it completes, rests on documents published after this article's date**, as the X-76 and X-69 through X-75 articles said for themselves. **The survey also reaches past the date**, its latest works being of 2026, among them the vertical-flight studies, NASA's presentation of RAVEN of May 2026 and the X-56A flutter workshop paper, which the review discusses as current literature for a reader of 2026 rather than as knowledge available on 16 December 2025.

### Historical Fact

The allocation dates, designations, contractors and sponsors of the register's rows, the register's notes on the X-50A, XQ-58A, XQ-67A and the other out-of-sequence drone numbers, and DARPA's statement of why it chose 76 are historical facts from primary documents. **The facts about individual aircraft are the earlier articles' and carry those articles' sources.**

### Measured From the Ledger and the Register

The counts of outcomes, design crews, keystone classes, ground-comparison verdicts and reasons for not flying are measurements over the ledger. The relation's totality, its two failures to be a function and its four failures of injectivity are measurements over the ledger and the register. The rank correlation, the pointer walk and the officiality split are measurements over the register. **Each is reproducible from the saved files by the calculation script, and none depends on a judgement made after the counting.**

### Statistical Analysis

The index of dispersion and its chi-square test, the Wilson intervals, Fisher's exact tests and the entropy of sponsorship are standard methods applied to the counts. **Their assumptions are stated where they are used**, the dispersion test assuming independent decades under a constant rate, and Fisher's test conditioning on the table's margins.

### Classification, Stated as Such

**The keystone class of each vehicle and the reason a vehicle did not fly are classifications made by one reader per article**, and the purpose result rests on them. The crewed result rests on the articles' statements and on a rule that a missile or rocket carries nobody, and it survives the most adverse assignment of the eight vehicles whose crew is not stated.

### Inference

That the clusters are institutional rather than budgetary is an inference from the coincidence of the second cluster with new sponsors, and no budget series was tested against the allocation dates. **That a number announced as a message is a different object from a sequence index is an interpretation**, and the evidence for it is the change in how the reason was published, from a compiler's note in 2002 to a headline in 2026.

### Errors in the Series That This Article Found

**Reading seventy articles as data found two errors in them.** Both were in articles about single aircraft, and both were repaired in those articles on 3 October 2026, when this article was written.

- **The X-49 article dated the filling of the vacancy at 49 to 2004**, which is the year the programme moved from the Navy to the Army, while the register dates the X-49A's allocation to 23 May 2003. **The article now gives the register's date** \[[X-49][related_post_a346_piasecki_x49]\] \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\].
- **The X-5 article contained a paragraph whose details belonged to the X-4**, a first aircraft that made only ten flights and was called a lemon, a second that made twenty contractor flights, and a handover in February 1950, while the same article dated the X-5's first flights to June and December 1951. The details match those the X-4 article gives for its own aircraft \[[X-4][related_post_a301_northrop_x4]\]. **The paragraph has been replaced with the X-5's record from the NASA history of its flight research centre**, which gives the contractor programme ending in October 1951, a six-flight Air Force evaluation in December 1951 and 133 flights by the NACA from 1952 to late 1955 \[[X-5][related_post_a302_bell_x5]\] \[[Hallion 1984][research_hallion_1984]\].

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Who chose the numbers is known for three of them**, the X-50, whose number was requested by DARPA or by Boeing depending on the account, the F-47, whose choice released Air Force public affairs correspondence attributes to General Allvin \[[X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block]\], and the X-76, whose number DARPA announced. For the rest the record says which office allocated the number and not who asked for it. **Whether the share of vehicles built to measure has fallen cannot be settled at the size of this series.** A difference of the size observed would need about 131 vehicles in each period to be detected four times in five at the 5 percent level, against the 29 and 35 the series has.

## Out of Scope

This article does not revisit any aircraft's engineering, which the seventy articles before it did, and it does not resolve any question those articles left open. It does not survey the literature of any one aircraft's subject. It does not treat the pre-1946 designation systems, foreign research aircraft, or the research aircraft that carried NASA rather than military designations, as the first article excluded them. **It does not test the clusters against budget data**, which would need a budget series the series never assembled. **It does not attempt the documentary-trace count it abandoned**, and a reader who wants that measurement will need to curate title matches by hand rather than by query.

## Conclusion

**The X designation began as a count of instruments, and it still mostly is one.** Sixty-five of its seventy-six numbers went to a vehicle, the numbers the register can test kept their order in every case but one, and the share of vehicles built to measure something did not fall in any way the record can detect. The first article's model of the research aircraft as an instrument describes about two fifths of the X vehicles across the whole series, and the record cannot show that it describes fewer of them now than it did in the 1950s.

**What changed is who is aboard, who pays, who can read the description, and how the number is chosen.** Of the X vehicles whose crew is recorded, seven in ten carried a pilot before 1990, and nearly every aircraft among them did, and since 1990 about one in four has. The sponsors went from the Air Force and NACA to a spread of agencies and laboratories. The register stopped carrying the government's own description of each research aircraft after the X-60. **And the number went from being assigned to being chosen**, first quietly in 2002 for a pun on fifty-fifty, then openly in 2025 for 1776, by an agency announcing its choice as the news.

**The series ends at a test the X-69 through X-75 article set** \[[X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block]\]. The next research designation is the X-69A if the X-49 precedent governs, since a passed number was assigned to the next request in 2003, and the X-77A if the 2020 rule governs, since it defines the next number from the last approved one. **Whichever it is will say whether the X-76 was a skip or a new ceiling**, and so whether the designation is still a count with a celebration in it, or has become a sequence of chosen symbols. Seventy-one articles ago this series opened by saying that a research aircraft is a machine built to measure one thing. **The designation that marks it turned out to measure something too**, which is the institutions that kept it.
